items.plain: Asked how to get past suffering, the answer is: faith carries you across the flood, diligence across the deluge, energy past suffering, and wisdom makes you pure.
items.core_idea: Faith, diligence, energy and wisdom carry you past suffering.

items.plain: You earn wealth by being responsible, doing what is fitting and working hard. Being truthful earns you a good name, and giving keeps your friends.
items.core_idea: Hard work earns wealth, truth reputation, giving friendship.

items.plain: The greatest patience is when a strong person puts up with a weak one; the weak have no choice. Foolish strength is really weakness, but someone strong and guarded by the teaching cannot be beaten.
items.core_idea: True patience is the strong bearing with the weak.

items.plain: A person should keep working until the goal is reached. For reaching a worthwhile goal, nothing is better than patience.
items.core_idea: Patience is the best way to reach a goal.

items.plain: You harvest whatever kind of seed you plant. Those who do good receive good, and those who do bad receive bad.
items.core_idea: You reap what you sow.

items.plain: Once anger is killed you sleep easily and sorrow goes. Anger has a poisonous root and a sweet tip; the noble ones praise destroying it, because then sorrow ends.
items.core_idea: Killing anger brings peaceful sleep and ends sorrow.

items.plain: My mind is not easily upset or pulled into turmoil. When anger comes it does not last, I do not speak harshly or boast, and I hold myself back for my own good.
items.core_idea: A steady mind lets anger pass without harsh words.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants there are two kinds of fool: one who does not see their own mistake, and one who will not accept another's apology. The wise do both.
items.core_idea: Admit your mistakes and accept others' apologies.

items.plain: Do not let anger rule you, and do not get angry at angry people. The noble ones are always kind and harmless, and anger crushes bad people like a mountain.
items.core_idea: Do not let anger rule you.

items.plain: A lazy person lives miserably among bad qualities and misses their heart's highest goal; an energetic person lives happily and reaches it. The best is reached only by the best effort, never the worst.
items.core_idea: Energy, not laziness, reaches the heart's highest goal.

items.plain: Whoever lies is full of fear and hostility in this life and lives to come, and suffers mental pain and sadness. Whoever stops lying is freed from that fear and hostility.
items.core_idea: Lying brings fear and pain; honesty calms it.

items.plain: A big fire goes out when no more fuel is added. In the same way, some things feed our grasping, and when you focus on their drawbacks, your craving stops.
items.core_idea: Starve craving by seeing the drawbacks of its fuel.

items.plain: What we call the mind or consciousness keeps arising as one thing and ending as another, day and night, like a monkey in a forest grabbing one branch after another.
items.core_idea: The mind jumps restlessly like a monkey between branches.

items.plain: A thirsty man is offered a delicious drink that is laced with poison and would kill him. He thinks it over, chooses another drink, and leaves the poisoned one alone, avoiding death.
items.core_idea: Refuse pleasant things that bring lasting harm.
items.extended_text: Suppose there was a bronze goblet of beverage that had a nice color, aroma, and flavor. But it was mixed with poison. Then along comes a man struggling in the oppressive heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. They’d say to him: ‘Here, my man, this bronze goblet of beverage has a nice color, aroma, and flavor. But it’s mixed with poison. Drink it if you like. If you drink it, its nice color, aroma, and flavor will refresh you. But drinking it will result in death or deadly pain.’ Then that man might think: ‘I can allay my thirst with a fermented drink of beer, buttermilk, salt lassi, or salted infusion. But in any case, I shouldn’t drink that beverage, for it would be for my lasting harm and suffering.’ He’d put that beverage down. After appraisal, he wouldn’t drink it, and it wouldn’t result in death or deadly pain. In the same way, there were ascetics and brahmins of the past who saw the things that seem nice and pleasant in the world as impermanent, as suffering, as not-self, as diseased, and as dangerous. They gave up craving.

items.plain: A torch dropped in dry grass does no harm if quickly put out. Likewise, if a seeker quickly drops a corrupt thought, they live happily now and can expect a good rebirth after death.
items.core_idea: Put out a bad thought quickly, like a dropped torch.

items.plain: People with low convictions gather with others like them, and people with good convictions gather with others like them.
items.core_idea: People are drawn to those who share their convictions.

items.plain: Mixing with people tangles you up. Like clinging to a small log at sea, you sink if you rely on a lazy person, so avoid them and live with the noble, devoted and energetic.
items.core_idea: Avoid lazy company; keep company with the energetic and wise.

items.plain: Over countless lives you have shed more tears than all the water in the four oceans, grieving the deaths of family, losses of every kind, and being parted from those you love.
items.core_idea: Across endless lives your tears outweigh the oceans.

items.plain: When you see someone suffering and in distress, remind yourself that over the long round of lives, you too have been through exactly the same.
items.core_idea: You too have suffered as others suffer.

items.plain: Anyone with faith, conscience, prudence, energy and wisdom in good qualities will only grow in them, day and night, just as the waxing moon keeps growing in beauty and size.
items.core_idea: Good qualities grow steadily like the waxing moon.

items.plain: Possessions, honour and popularity are harsh and bitter, and block the way to the highest freedom. So train yourself to give them up and not let them fill your mind.
items.core_idea: Wealth, honour and fame are obstacles to freedom.

items.plain: A true person's meditation stays steady whether they are honoured or ignored. They keep meditating with clear understanding and rejoice in the end of clinging.
items.core_idea: Honour or neglect cannot shake a true person.

items.plain: Just as a banana plant, bamboo and reed are destroyed by their own fruit, honour destroys a bad person.
items.core_idea: Honour ruins an unworthy person.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that giving huge gifts of rice three times a day is less fruitful than developing a loving heart even for a moment, the time it takes to milk a cow.
items.core_idea: A moment of love outweighs great gifts.

items.plain: We will be grateful and thankful, and never forget even a small kindness done for us.
items.core_idea: Remember even small kindnesses with gratitude.

items.plain: Extinguishment, freedom from all suffering, cannot be reached by someone slack or weak in effort.
items.core_idea: Freedom from suffering demands strong effort.

items.plain: Geese, herons, peacocks, elephants and deer differ in size, yet all fear the lion. Among people too, a small person who is wise is truly great, not a fool with a fine body.
items.core_idea: Wisdom, not size, makes a person great.

items.plain: Why are you angry, Tissa? Do not be. It is better not to be angry, because the spiritual life is lived to remove anger, pride and contempt.
items.core_idea: The spiritual life exists to remove anger.

items.plain: Truly living alone means letting go of the past, giving up the future, and ending desire and greed for life in the present.
items.core_idea: Living alone means releasing past, future and present craving.

items.plain: An old, sick man asks the Buddha for advice. The Buddha agrees the body is frail and says to train like this: though my body is sick, my mind will be healthy.
items.core_idea: Though the body is ailing, keep the mind healthy.

items.plain: Arguing with people means engaging in talk like: you don't understand, I do; you're wrong, I'm right; your view is refuted, get out of that if you can.
items.core_idea: Quarrelling is the contest of 'I'm right, you're wrong'.

items.plain: Carrying the burden is suffering, and putting it down is happiness. Someone who lays down the heavy burden without picking up another, and pulls out craving by the root, is satisfied and at peace.
items.core_idea: Laying down the burden of craving brings peace.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants to give up what is not theirs, because letting it go will bring them wellbeing and happiness.
items.core_idea: Let go of what is not yours.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants to be their own island and refuge, relying on nothing else, and to make the teaching their island and refuge.
items.core_idea: Be your own refuge, with the teaching as refuge.

items.plain: An untaught person worries over things not worth worrying about, fearing what might not be or not be theirs. A learned disciple of the noble ones does not worry about such things.
items.core_idea: The wise do not worry about losing what isn't theirs.

items.plain: When you cling, you are caught by Māra; when you do not cling, you are free of the Wicked One.
items.core_idea: Clinging binds you; letting go frees you.

items.plain: Give up desire for anything that does not last.
items.core_idea: Do not desire what is impermanent.

items.plain: How happy the perfected ones are! They have no craving, no sense of 'I am', and no delusion. Their minds are calm and clear, nothing in the world clings to them, and they are pure.
items.core_idea: The perfected ones are happy, free of craving and ego.

items.plain: Living on alms is the lowest way of life, and people mock beggars. Yet sincere men choose it, not from fear or debt, but because they are overwhelmed by suffering and hope to end it entirely.
items.core_idea: Seekers embrace poverty to end suffering.

items.plain: Both before and now, all I teach is suffering and the ending of suffering.
items.core_idea: The teaching is suffering and its ending.

items.plain: The Buddha tells Vakkali there is no point in seeing his decaying body. Whoever sees the teaching sees the Buddha, and whoever sees the Buddha sees the teaching.
items.core_idea: To see the teaching is to see the Buddha.

items.plain: Like a lamp that goes out when its oil and wick run out, a dying person knows the end of body and life is near, and understands that all feeling, no longer relished, will simply cool.
items.core_idea: At death, unrelished feeling simply cools like a spent lamp.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants he does not argue with the world; the world argues with him. When your words agree with the teaching, you have no quarrel with anyone.
items.core_idea: Speak in line with truth and quarrel with no one.

items.plain: A lotus grows in water yet rises above it with no water clinging to it. In the same way, though born and raised in the world, the Buddha lives above it, untouched by it.
items.core_idea: Live in the world untouched by it, like a lotus.

items.plain: A bubble on rainwater forms and bursts at once; looked at closely it is empty and without substance. A mendicant who looks closely at feeling sees it is just as empty.
items.core_idea: Feelings are as empty as water bubbles.

items.plain: The Buddha taught that the body is like foam, feeling like a bubble, perception like a mirage, choices like a banana plant and consciousness like an illusion: examined closely, all are hollow.
items.core_idea: Body and mind are hollow when examined closely.

items.plain: Regularly look at your own mind and recognise it has long been stained by greed, hate and delusion. Beings are corrupted when the mind is corrupted, and purified when the mind is purified.
items.core_idea: Purity and corruption begin in the mind.

items.plain: A mason sees his adze handle wearing away but cannot tell how much went each day, only that it is worn. Likewise, a committed mendicant cannot measure daily progress, but knows the defilements are wearing away.
items.core_idea: Spiritual progress is unseen day to day but real.

items.plain: Children treasure sandcastles while they still want them, then smash them once the desire is gone. In the same way, break apart body, feeling, perception, choices and consciousness, and work to end craving, which is extinguishment.
items.core_idea: Smash attachments like outgrown sandcastles to end craving.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants the eye does not last, and what does not last is suffering and not self. See it truly: this is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.
items.core_idea: The impermanent is not mine, not me, not self.

items.plain: Whatever you imagine a thing to be, or imagine as 'mine', turns into something else. The world clings to existence and delights only in it, yet it keeps changing.
items.core_idea: Whatever we cling to as ours keeps changing.

items.plain: There are attractive, pleasing sights. If a mendicant does not welcome or cling to them, delight in them stops, and when that delight stops, the Buddha says, suffering stops.
items.core_idea: Ending delight in pleasures ends suffering.

items.plain: The Buddha tells Ānanda the world is called empty because it is empty of a self or anything belonging to a self: the senses, their objects, and every feeling are empty in this way.
items.core_idea: The world is empty of self.

items.plain: Whoever depends on things wavers; whoever does not depend is still. Stillness brings calm, calm ends leaning and coming and going, and with that there is no dying, rebirth, or any life: this is the end of suffering.
items.core_idea: Without dependence there is stillness and an end of suffering.

items.plain: The Buddha asks Puṇṇa what he will think if the rough people he is going to live among insult him. Puṇṇa says he will think them kind, because at least they do not hit him.
items.core_idea: Meet insult with gratitude that it is not worse.

items.plain: When you see pleasant and unpleasant sights, let go of all desire for the pleasant, without hating what you dislike.
items.core_idea: Desire nothing pleasant; hate nothing unpleasant.

items.plain: Whether a smell is sweet or foul, or a taste sweet or bitter, drop aversion to the unpleasant and do not give in to desire or attachment for the pleasant.
items.core_idea: Meet pleasant and unpleasant senses without craving or aversion.

items.plain: When you see something and fix on its pleasant side, you lose mindfulness and cling with desire. Feelings multiply, greed and cruelty damage the mind, and piling up suffering this way, you are far from extinguishment.
items.core_idea: Clinging to pleasant sights piles up suffering.

items.plain: Seeing something with mindfulness, you feel no desire and do not cling. Even while experiencing it you wear suffering away instead of piling it up, and so you are close to extinguishment.
items.core_idea: Mindful seeing wears suffering away.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that the end of the world cannot be known, seen or reached by travelling, yet suffering cannot end without reaching the end of the world.
items.core_idea: The world's end is reached within, not by travel.

items.plain: Eating in moderation means a mendicant reflects that food is not for fun or vanity, but only to keep the body going, avoid harm and support spiritual practice, easing hunger without creating new discomfort.
items.core_idea: Eat to sustain the body, not for indulgence.

items.plain: A calm, clear, untroubled mind that is kind to all creatures is the path to becoming divine.
items.core_idea: A calm, kind mind is the path to the divine.

items.plain: A mendicant who sees something does not hold on to it if it is pleasant or dislike it if it is unpleasant. They live mindful of the body, with a boundless heart.
items.core_idea: Neither grasp the pleasant nor resent the unpleasant.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that gods and humans love and enjoy sights, but when those sights fade and end, they suffer.
items.core_idea: Loving what fades leads to suffering.

items.plain: What other people call happiness, the noble ones call suffering, and what others call suffering, the noble ones know to be happiness.
items.core_idea: The wise see happiness and suffering in reverse.

items.plain: Here are trees to sit under and empty huts. The Buddha urges the mendicants to meditate, not to be careless, and not to regret it later: this is his instruction.
items.core_idea: Meditate now, so you will not regret it later.

items.plain: The eye is an ocean whose currents are sights. Whoever overcomes those currents, with all their waves and dangers, has crossed over and stands on solid ground on the far shore.
items.core_idea: Master the currents of the senses to cross over.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that a monk or nun who still has greed, hate and delusion is overwhelmed even by trivial sights, let alone compelling ones, because those roots remain.
items.core_idea: While greed remains, even small sights overwhelm the mind.

items.plain: Two oxen joined by a yoke are not each other's yoke; the yoke binds them. Likewise the eye and sights do not bind each other; what binds is the desire and greed arising between them.
items.core_idea: Desire, not the senses, is what binds us.

items.plain: Eating in moderation means a mendicant eats only to sustain the body and support practice, not for pleasure, like putting ointment on a wound only to heal it, or oiling an axle only to carry a load.
items.core_idea: Eat only to sustain the body, as ointment heals.

items.plain: Someone in a thorny thicket moves carefully and mindfully to avoid the thorns. In the same way, in the Noble One's training, whatever in the world seems nice and pleasant is called a thorn.
items.core_idea: Pleasant things are thorns on the spiritual path.

items.plain: A person asks different people what a parrot tree looks like and gets different answers, black, red, pod-laden, leafy, each true of the tree at the time that person saw it.
items.core_idea: Different true answers come from different vantage points.
items.extended_text: Mendicant, suppose a person had never seen a parrot tree before. They’d go up to someone who had seen a parrot tree and ask them, ‘My man, what’s a parrot tree like?’ They’d say, ‘A parrot tree is blackish, like a charred stump.’ Now, at that time a parrot tree may well have been just as that person saw it. Not content with that answer, that person would go up to a series of other people and receive the following answers: ‘A parrot tree is reddish, like a scrap of meat.’ ‘A parrot tree has flaking bark and burst pods, like a lebbeck tree.’ ‘A parrot tree has luxuriant, shady foliage, like a banyan.’ Now, at each of those times a parrot tree may well have been just as those people saw them. In the same way, those true persons each answered according to what they were focused on when their vision was well purified.

items.plain: The 'abyss' is really painful bodily feeling. An untaught person facing pain wails and falls into confusion, finding no footing; a learned disciple of the noble ones meets pain without lament and finds firm footing.
items.core_idea: Meeting pain calmly gives footing in the abyss.

items.plain: If you cannot bear painful bodily feelings and tremble and wail at them, you will not find your footing in the abyss. If you can endure them without trembling, you will.
items.core_idea: Enduring pain without trembling gives you footing.

items.plain: When an untaught person feels bodily pain and adds grief and confusion, they feel two pains, physical and mental, like someone shot by one arrow and then a second.
items.core_idea: Mental distress is a second arrow after pain.

items.plain: A learned person who has understood the teaching sees this world and the next clearly. Desirable things do not stir their mind, and undesirable things do not repel them.
items.core_idea: The wise are unmoved by liking and disliking.

items.plain: Like a lamp that goes out when oil and wick run out, a dying mendicant knows the end of body and life is near, and understands that every feeling, no longer enjoyed, will simply cool.
items.core_idea: At death, feelings no longer enjoyed simply cool.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that winds of every kind blow from all directions, dusty or clean, cool or warm, weak or strong. In the same way, pleasant, painful and neutral feelings arise in the body.
items.core_idea: Feelings come and go like winds.

items.plain: A guest house takes in travellers from every direction and of every class. In the same way, pleasant, painful and neutral feelings come and stay in this body.
items.core_idea: The body hosts feelings like a guest house.

items.plain: The Buddha says he has explained feelings in many ways. Those who will not accept what is well said will quarrel and wound each other; those who accept it will live in harmony, blending like milk and water.
items.core_idea: Accepting what is well said brings harmony, not quarrels.

items.plain: Sāriputta says that in this path, going forth is hard; once gone forth, being content is hard; once content, practising the teaching is hard. But whoever practises it will soon be perfected.
items.core_idea: Each stage is hard, but true practice soon succeeds.

items.plain: Someone who has given up greed, hate and delusion is not annoyed by others and does not show annoyance, so they are seen as gentle. That is why some people are considered gentle.
items.core_idea: Gentleness comes from giving up greed, hate and delusion.

items.plain: Someone reflects: the Buddha condemns lying, I have lied, that was wrong and I regret it, but I cannot undo it. So they stop lying from now on. That is how to leave a bad deed behind.
items.core_idea: Admit the wrong, stop repeating it, and move past it.

items.plain: A chief admits he worries all day about his son living far away, and would grieve terribly if harm came to him. The Buddha says this shows that all suffering is rooted in desire.
items.core_idea: Desire is the root of suffering.

items.plain: One who has gone forth should avoid two extremes: indulging in sensual pleasure, which is low and pointless, and tormenting oneself, which is painful and pointless. The Buddha found the middle way between them, leading to peace and awakening.
items.core_idea: Avoid both indulgence and self-torment: take the middle way.

items.plain: Joy arises in them, and joy grows into rapture. With a rapturous mind the body becomes calm, a calm body feels bliss, and in bliss the mind settles into deep meditation.
items.core_idea: Joy leads step by step to deep meditative calm.

items.plain: Ānanda says good friends and companions are half the spiritual life. The Buddha corrects him: good friends and companions are the whole of the spiritual life.
items.core_idea: Good friends are the whole of the spiritual life.

items.plain: Right speech means avoiding speech that is false, divisive, harsh or pointless.
items.core_idea: Right speech avoids lies, slander, harshness and idle talk.

items.plain: A pot without a stand tips over easily, but a pot on a stand is hard to knock over. The mind is the same: without support it is easily upset, with support it is hard to upset.
items.core_idea: A mind with firm support is hard to upset.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that just as dawn comes before sunrise, good friendship comes before the noble eightfold path.
items.core_idea: Good friendship is the dawn of the spiritual path.

items.plain: Every animal's footprint fits inside an elephant's, so the elephant's is called the greatest. In the same way, all good qualities are rooted in diligence and meet in it, so diligence is the best.
items.core_idea: Diligence is the root of all good qualities.

items.plain: The Buddha asks the mendicants where a tree leaning east would fall if cut at the root. They answer: in the direction it leans.
items.core_idea: You fall the way you lean.
items.extended_text: “Mendicants, suppose a tree slants, slopes, and inclines to the east. If it was cut off at the root, where would it fall?” “Sir, it would fall in the direction that it slants, slopes, and inclines.” “In the same way, a mendicant who develops and cultivates the noble eightfold path slants, slopes, and inclines to extinguishment.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants there are three kinds of comparing oneself: thinking 'I'm better', 'I'm equal', or 'I'm worse'.
items.core_idea: Better, equal or worse: all comparison is conceit.

items.plain: What makes ill will arise and grow? Dwelling again and again, unwisely, on what we find repellent feeds ill will and makes it grow.
items.core_idea: Dwelling on what repels you feeds ill will.

items.plain: A mendicant sees a pleasing sight without desire or greed, and an unpleasant one without dismay, irritation or anger. Either way, their mind and body stay steady, settled and free.
items.core_idea: Stay steady whether sights please or displease.

items.plain: The Buddha asks the sick Kassapa if he is getting better and his pain easing. Kassapa answers honestly that he is not well: his pain is terrible and growing worse.
items.core_idea: Honestly admitting that pain is growing.
items.extended_text: “I hope you’re keeping well, Kassapa, I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.” “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.” “Kassapa, I’ve rightly explained these seven awakening factors. When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to extinguishment.

items.plain: Gold mixed with iron, copper, tin, lead or silver is brittle and dull. In the same way, sensual desire, ill will, drowsiness, restlessness and doubt make the mind brittle and unable to settle in meditation.
items.core_idea: Five hindrances corrupt the mind like impurities in gold.

items.plain: What starves ill will, so it does not arise or grow? The heart's release by love: dwelling on it again and again, wisely, starves ill will.
items.core_idea: Cultivating love starves ill will.

items.plain: When the mind is restless, it is the right time to develop tranquility, deep meditation and equanimity, because these easily settle a restless mind.
items.core_idea: Calm a restless mind with tranquility and equanimity.

items.plain: In a muddy bowl of water in the dark, you cannot see your reflection. Likewise, when your heart is sunk in doubt, you cannot see what is good for yourself, for others, or for both.
items.core_idea: Doubt clouds the mind like muddy water.

items.plain: In a clear bowl of water in the light, you see your reflection plainly. Likewise, when your heart is free of doubt, you clearly see what is good for yourself, for others, and for both.
items.core_idea: A mind free of doubt sees clearly, like clear water.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the direct path to purify beings, get past sorrow and tears, end pain and sadness, and reach extinguishment.
items.core_idea: Mindfulness is the direct path beyond sorrow.

items.plain: Careful monkeys see the sticky tar trap and keep away. A reckless monkey grabs it and gets stuck, then grabs with his other hand to free himself and gets stuck again.
items.core_idea: Struggling with a trap only entangles you further.

items.plain: The Buddha tells Sāriputta that someone whose mind is free is a great person, and someone whose mind is not free is not.
items.core_idea: Greatness is a free mind.

items.plain: Ānanda grieves for Sāriputta, who guided and counselled him, taught, encouraged and inspired him, never tired of teaching the Dhamma, and supported his companions on the path.
items.core_idea: Grieving a beloved teacher and guide.

items.plain: The Buddha reminds Ānanda that he taught we must be parted from everyone and everything we love. Whatever is born and made must wear out; it cannot be otherwise.
items.core_idea: All we love must pass; nothing made can last.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants the assembly feels empty now that Sāriputta and Moggallāna have passed away. It never felt empty before, and wherever they stayed, he had no worry.
items.core_idea: Even the Buddha feels the emptiness of loss.

items.plain: You look after others by looking after yourself through meditation, and look after yourself by looking after others through patience, harmlessness, love and sympathy. Caring for yourself and caring for others go together.
items.core_idea: Caring for yourself and caring for others go together.

items.plain: A mendicant is aware when they know their feelings, thoughts and perceptions as they arise, as they stay, and as they pass away.
items.core_idea: Awareness is watching experiences arise, stay and pass.

items.plain: Sadness arises from something experienced as sad. When you are sad, you know that you are sad, and when its cause ends, you know the sadness has ended too.
items.core_idea: Know sadness as it arises and as it ends.

items.plain: When young you are bound to grow old, when healthy to fall ill, when alive to die. The skin loses its brightness, the limbs wrinkle, the body stoops, and the senses decline.
items.core_idea: Youth, health and life all give way to decline.

items.plain: Curse this wretched old age that makes the lovely body ugly and wears it down. Even if you live a hundred years, you will still die; death spares no one.
items.core_idea: Old age wears us down and death spares no one.

items.plain: After trying, remembering, meditating and reflecting wisely again and again, a noble disciple becomes confident: once I only heard of these things, now I experience and see them directly.
items.core_idea: Repeated practice turns hearsay into direct experience.

items.plain: The four right efforts are working hard to keep bad qualities from arising, to give up bad qualities that have arisen, to make good qualities arise, and to keep good ones growing to fullness.
items.core_idea: Prevent and abandon bad; grow and keep good.

items.plain: Enthusiasm is too slack when it comes with laziness, and too tense when it comes with restlessness.
items.core_idea: Effort fails when too slack or too tense.

items.plain: Asked how he keeps physical pain from taking over his mind, the gravely ill Anuruddha says he keeps his mind firmly established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.
items.core_idea: Mindfulness keeps pain from occupying the mind.

items.plain: To practise mindfulness of breathing, a mendicant sits somewhere quiet, straight and cross-legged, and simply breathes in and out mindfully, knowing when each breath is heavy or light.
items.core_idea: Sit still and know each breath as it comes.

items.plain: Like a lamp going out when its oil and wick are spent, a dying person knows the end of body and life is near, and understands that all feeling, no longer enjoyed, will simply cool.
items.core_idea: At death, feelings no longer enjoyed simply cool.

items.plain: As an unseasonal storm settles summer dust at once, meditation on breathing, when developed, is peaceful and blissful, and settles bad qualities the moment they arise.
items.core_idea: Mindful breathing settles bad states like rain settles dust.

items.plain: Those with faith, good conduct, confidence and a clear view of the truth eventually reach happiness, the goal of the spiritual life.
items.core_idea: Faith, ethics and insight lead in time to happiness.

items.plain: A noble disciple reflects: I want to live and be happy and I hate pain, so I would not want to be killed. Others feel the same. How can I do to them what I would hate done to me?
items.core_idea: Do not inflict on others what you would hate yourself.

items.plain: When a pot of ghee breaks underwater, the shards sink but the ghee rises. Likewise, when someone long steeped in faith, ethics, learning, generosity and wisdom dies, the body decays and is eaten, but the mind rises higher.
items.core_idea: A good mind rises when the body perishes.

items.plain: Whoever has firm faith in the Buddha, good conduct loved by the noble ones, confidence in the Saṅgha and right view is truly rich; their life is not wasted. So the wise should devote themselves to these.
items.core_idea: Faith, ethics and right view make a life rich.

items.plain: Living diligently, joy arises and grows into rapture. Rapture calms the body, a calm body feels bliss, bliss settles the mind in deep meditation, and then the truth becomes clear.
items.core_idea: Diligence leads through joy and calm to clarity.

items.plain: Someone who seeks merit and is grounded in good develops the path to freedom from death. Having reached the heart of the teaching and delighting in ending, they do not tremble when the King of Death approaches.
items.core_idea: One who has realised the teaching does not fear death.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants not to think bad thoughts, such as sensual, malicious or cruel ones, because they do not help the spiritual life or lead to peace, insight and awakening.
items.core_idea: Avoid thoughts that do not lead to peace.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants not to get into arguments of the 'I'm right, you're wrong, your view is refuted' kind, because such talk does not help the spiritual life or lead to peace and awakening.
items.core_idea: Don't argue about who is right; it leads nowhere.

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants to avoid two extremes: indulging in sensual pleasure, which is low and pointless, and tormenting oneself, which is painful and pointless. He found the middle way, leading to peace and awakening.
items.core_idea: The middle way avoids indulgence and self-torment.

items.plain: This is the noble truth of suffering: birth, ageing, illness and death are suffering; being with what you dislike, parted from what you like, and not getting what you want are suffering.
items.core_idea: Life's losses and frustrations are the truth of suffering.

items.plain: Holding a few leaves, the Buddha says that what he has taught is like those few leaves compared with the forest: he knows far more, but leaves it unsaid because it does not help the spiritual life.
items.core_idea: Teach only what helps; the rest is left unsaid.

items.plain: A deep-rooted pillar cannot be shaken by storms from any side. In the same way, those who truly understand suffering, its origin, its ending and the path do not look to other teachers, thinking they must know better.
items.core_idea: Those who truly understand stand firm, needing no other's authority.

items.plain: The poet tells God: you have made me endless, emptying and refilling this fragile vessel with new life, playing new melodies through me. Your touch fills my heart with joy, and your gifts keep pouring into my small hands.
items.core_idea: God endlessly refills and plays through a small life.

items.plain: When God asks the poet to sing, his heart nearly bursts with pride and tears come as he looks at God's face. All that is harsh in his life melts into harmony, and his worship flies like a happy bird.
items.core_idea: Singing for God turns life's discord into harmony.

items.plain: The poet vows to God, the life of his life, to keep body pure, thoughts truthful and heart loving, since God touches, enlightens and dwells in him, and to show God in his deeds, since God gives him strength.
items.core_idea: Live purely because God dwells within you.

items.plain: The poet asks God for a moment to sit beside him; work can wait. Away from God his heart finds no rest and work is endless toil. Summer has come: now is the time to sit quietly with God.
items.core_idea: Pause from work to sit quietly with God.

fix.display_text:
I ask for a moment’s indulgence to sit by thy side. The works that I have in hand I will finish afterwards.

Away from the sight of thy face my heart knows no rest nor respite, and my work becomes an endless toil in a shoreless sea of toil.

Today the summer has come at my window with its sighs and murmurs; and the bees are plying their minstrelsy at the court of the flowering grove.

Now it is time to sit quiet, face to face with thee, and to sing dedication of life in this silent and overflowing leisure.

items.plain: The poet asks God to pick the little flower of his life now, before it wilts. Though pale and faintly scented, let it serve God, for he fears the time for offering will pass.
items.core_idea: Offer your life now, before the time passes.

items.plain: The poet's song has dropped its ornaments, which would come between him and God. His poet's pride dies; sitting at God's feet, he asks only for a simple life, like a reed flute for God to fill.
items.core_idea: A simple life lets God's music through.

items.plain: A child in fine robes and jewels cannot enjoy play, afraid to get dirty or move. Finery is no gain if it shuts you off from the earth's healthy dust and the shared life of ordinary people.
items.core_idea: Finery that cuts you off from life is worthless.

items.plain: Carrying yourself on your own shoulders is foolish, like begging at your own door. Leave your burdens with the one who bears all, without regret. Desire defiles what it touches; accept only what sacred love offers.
items.core_idea: Lay your burdens down and accept only what love gives.

items.plain: The poet tells God that God's feet rest among the poorest, lowliest and lost. His bowing, his pride and his heart cannot reach down to where God walks humbly and keeps company with the companionless.
items.core_idea: God is found among the poorest and the lost.

items.plain: Stop chanting in a dark, shut temple: God is not there. God is with the farmer and road-builder, covered in dust, bound with all of creation. Come out and stand with God in toil and sweat.
items.core_idea: God is found in honest labour, not closed temples.

fix.display_text:
Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee!

He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones. He is with them in sun and in shower, and his garment is covered with dust. Put off thy holy mantle and even like him come down on the dusty soil!

Deliverance? Where is this deliverance to be found? Our master himself has joyfully taken upon him the bonds of creation; he is bound with us all for ever.

Come out of thy meditations and leave aside thy flowers and incense! What harm is there if thy clothes become tattered and stained? Meet him and stand by him in toil and in sweat of thy brow.

items.plain: The longest journey leads nearest to God, as the hardest training leads to the simplest tune. You must knock at every stranger's door to reach your own. After searching far, the poet closes his eyes and finds God here.
items.core_idea: The longest search leads back home to God within.

items.plain: The song I came to sing is still unsung. I have spent my days tuning my instrument, and the time and words were never right. There is only the ache of longing, like a bud that has not opened.
items.core_idea: The ache of a life's song still unsung.

items.plain: The poet tells God: my desires are many, but you have always saved me by refusing them. That firm mercy is making me worthy of your simple, great gifts, sky, light, body, life and mind, and of your full acceptance.
items.core_idea: God's refusals are a mercy that saves us.

items.plain: Invited to the world's festival, I have been blessed by all I saw and heard, and played my part as best I could. Now I ask God whether it is time to see God's face and greet God silently.
items.core_idea: Having played my part, I am ready to meet God.

items.plain: I am only waiting to give myself up to love at last. Others try to bind me with laws and blame me as careless, perhaps rightly; the busy have gone home angry, but I still wait for love.
items.core_idea: Waiting, above all else, to surrender to love.

items.plain: As clouds darken, the poet asks love why he is left waiting alone. In busy hours he is with the crowd, but on this lonely day he hopes only for God and cannot bear the rainy hours without God.
items.core_idea: Longing for God on a dark, lonely day.

items.plain: If God does not speak, the poet will fill his heart with God's silence and endure it, waiting patiently like the night. Morning will surely come, the darkness will lift, and God's voice will pour down in golden streams.
items.core_idea: Wait patiently through silence; morning will come.

items.plain: When the lotus bloomed, my mind was wandering and I missed it. A faint fragrance stirred a longing in me, but I did not know then that this perfect sweetness had already blossomed deep within my own heart.
items.core_idea: What we long for already blooms within us.

fix.display_text:
On the day when the lotus bloomed, alas, my mind was straying, and I knew it not. My basket was empty and the flower remained unheeded.

Only now and again a sadness fell upon me, and I started up from my dream and felt a sweet trace of a strange fragrance in the south wind.

That vague sweetness made my heart ache with longing and it seemed to me that it was the eager breath of the summer seeking for its completion.

I knew not then that it was so near, that it was mine, and that this perfect sweetness had blossomed in the depth of my own heart.

items.plain: I must set out in my boat; idle hours pass on the shore. Spring is over and I linger with faded flowers. Why stare into emptiness? Can you not feel the thrill of a song from the far shore?
items.core_idea: Stop lingering; answer the call from the far shore.

items.plain: When the day is done, the poet asks God to cover him with darkness as gently as God puts the earth to sleep, and to lift the worn traveller's shame and renew his life like a flower overnight.
items.core_idea: Ask God for rest and renewal when you are spent.

items.plain: When I am weary, let me sleep without struggling, trusting God. Let me not force my tired spirit into a poor act of worship. It is God who brings night to tired eyes so they wake with fresh gladness.
items.core_idea: Rest trustingly; tiredness is renewed by sleep.

items.plain: Where is the light? Light it with the fire of desire! Thunder rolls, wind screams, and the night is black as stone. Do not let the hours pass in darkness; light the lamp of love with your life.
items.core_idea: Light the lamp of love with your own life.

items.plain: My chains are stubborn, yet breaking them hurts. I want freedom but feel ashamed to hope for it. I know God is my true wealth and friend, yet I cling to tinsel and fear my prayer might be granted.
items.core_idea: We long for freedom yet cling to what binds us.

items.plain: The self I wall in with my name weeps inside this prison. I keep building the wall higher, proud of it and sealing every gap, and in its shadow I lose sight of who I truly am.
items.core_idea: Building up our name hides our true being.

items.plain: On my way to meet God, someone follows me that I cannot escape. He stirs up dust and shouts over my every word. He is my own little self, and I am ashamed to come to God's door with him.
items.core_idea: The ego shadows us even on the way to God.

items.plain: A prisoner says he wanted to outdo everyone in wealth and power, hoarded his king's money, and woke a prisoner in his own treasure-house. He forged his chain himself to hold the world captive, and it holds him.
items.core_idea: The chains of greed and power we forge bind us.

items.plain: Those who love me here hold me tight and never leave me alone. God's greater love keeps me free and stays unseen; even if I forget to pray or keep God in my heart, God's love waits for mine.
items.core_idea: God's love sets us free and patiently waits.

items.plain: The poet asks that only enough of himself remain to call God his all, feel God everywhere and offer love every moment, with God's love as his only bond, carrying out God's purpose in his life.
items.core_idea: Keep only enough self to love God fully.

items.plain: The poet prays to God, his Father, that his country awake into a heaven of freedom: minds fearless, knowledge free, people undivided, words true, effort reaching for perfection, and reason not lost in dead habit.
items.core_idea: A prayer for a nation free, truthful and fearless.
